opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. The obvious answer is length: the hardest tasks are the ones that take skilled humans many hours, sometimes days. But length is a proxy. Time is just where a bunch of other kinds of difficulty show up.

When I look at what actually trips models up on the long tasks, a few things keep coming up.

**Long-horizon coherence.** You have to hold a plan together across hundreds of steps. You have to notice when an early decision was wrong and actually go back and revisit it, rather than patching around it forever. Models are often locally competent: any single step looks reasonable. But the trajectory drifts. They lose track of what they were trying to do, or they declare victory before they're actually done.

**Error recovery and self-verification.** On short tasks you can get away with not checking your work much. On long tasks, small errors compound. Strong humans constantly sanity-check things: "Does this output make sense? Did that test actually pass for the right reason?" Models are getting better at this, but it's still a big differentiator. A related failure is that they'll sometimes convince themselves something works when it doesn't.

**Underspecification and messiness.** Many of our hardest tasks are less like a clean exam problem and more like real work. The environment is a bit weird, the documentation is incomplete, and you have to figure out what "done" even means. We've seen that tasks rated as messier tend to be harder for models even after controlling for how long they take humans. That's one reason I'm cautious about extrapolating from benchmark performance to real-world usefulness. Real work is messier than most benchmarks.

**Genuine expertise or insight.** Some tasks require a specific idea that's hard to stumble into. You either know the trick or the relevant domain fact, or you have to reason your way to it. This was a big focus with GPQA, writing questions where even skilled non-experts with web access struggle. In agentic settings it looks a bit different, because the model can experiment. But there's still a category of tasks where brute-force iteration doesn't get you there.

One thing I'd flag is that difficulty for humans and difficulty for models aren't the same thing. We use human time as our main axis because it's interpretable and economically meaningful. But there are tasks that are tedious and slow for humans and relatively easy for models, and vice versa. So part of the work is being careful about what our difficulty measure is actually capturing, and not over-interpreting a single number.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's something I've thought about a lot, because when we were building GPQA, and then later with the agentic tasks at METR, the question of "what actually makes this hard" turned out to be surprisingly slippery.

The naive answer is that hard tasks require more knowledge. And that's partly true, but it's not really the interesting part. With GPQA, the whole design was that the questions should be ones where a PhD in the relevant field can answer them, but a very smart person from a different field, even with unlimited time and internet access, mostly can't. So it's not just "do you know the fact," it's "do you have the kind of deep, integrated understanding that lets you reason about something where the relevant information isn't neatly written down anywhere." The experts writing those questions were essentially trying to encode things that aren't Google-able, which turns out to be genuinely hard to do, and a lot of the question-writing process was iterating with validators to make sure the difficulty was coming from the right place rather than from, say, ambiguity or trick wording.

But I think the agentic setting reveals a different and maybe more important axis, which is something like task length, or the number of steps you have to chain together without making an unrecoverable mistake. When we look at tasks where models struggle and humans don't, very often it's not that any individual step is beyond the model. If you decomposed the task and handed each piece to the model in isolation, it could do most of them. The difficulty is in keeping track of state over a long horizon, noticing when you've gone down a wrong path, recovering from errors, and knowing when the thing you've built is actually done versus just looks done. Humans are kind of remarkable at this. A good engineer working for eight hours makes tons of small mistakes but catches them, and the task gets finished. Models have historically been much more brittle there, where one early mistake compounds and they never recover.

There's a third thing that I think gets underrated, which is that the hardest tasks are often ones where the success criterion is hard to verify, even for the person doing it. A math problem with a numerical answer has a clean signal. "Make this codebase actually work for the use case the user cares about" doesn't. And I think a lot of what we're measuring, when tasks get long and messy, is partly whether the model can construct its own feedback loop, test its own work, and be appropriately skeptical of itself. That's a capability that's sort of orthogonal to raw intelligence, and it's one where I think the gap between models and skilled humans has been closing, but it's been closing from a place where models were very bad at it.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say: hard isn't one thing. There's depth of expertise, there's horizon length and error recovery, and there's verification difficulty. And the tasks that are hardest for current systems tend to combine at least two of those.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different things that can make a task hard, and it’s useful to distinguish them. One is that it requires specialized knowledge. Another is that, even if you have all the relevant information, you need to put together a long chain of reasoning or notice a fairly subtle distinction.

And then there’s difficulty that comes from how we’ve written the question. Is it ambiguous? Are we asking for something in a confusing way? That’s generally not the kind of difficulty we want. Ideally, someone with the relevant expertise can look at the question and say, “Yes, there’s a clear answer, but getting there requires understanding the subject.”

So I wouldn’t equate a low model score with a good, hard evaluation. You also want evidence that the task is well-defined and that success tells you something meaningful about the capability you’re trying to measure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different things that can make a question hard, and it’s useful to separate them. One is just that it requires very specialized knowledge. Another is that, even if you have the relevant knowledge, you have to put it together in a way that isn’t obvious. And then there’s difficulty that comes from the question being ambiguous or poorly specified, which is generally something we want to avoid.

For GPQA, the idea was to get questions where an expert in the relevant field could reliably arrive at the answer, but someone without that expertise would struggle even with access to the internet. So you can’t just search for a phrase and find the answer—you need enough understanding to know which information matters and how to apply it.

But I’d be cautious about saying that this tells us exactly what makes those questions hard for a model. A question that’s difficult for a human might be easy for a model, or vice versa. The human comparisons help us characterize the questions, but they aren’t a complete explanation of what the model is doing.
